items.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
items.summary:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for. 

When the “ Monument Against Fascism ” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque. 

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.
items.t: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

items.title: The High Line Broaches British Empire in New Joint Exhibition
items.summary:
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Earth presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires. 

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty. 

Shahzia Sikander, still from “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026) (image courtesy the artist)
items.t: The High Line Broaches British Empire in New Joint Exhibition

items.title: Louis Vuitton Launches Three Fragrances as Part of Expansive Keith Haring Collection
items.summary:
As part of an expansive collection set to include ready-to-wear fashion, accessories, and a recently touted line of limited-edition Artycapucines handbags, Louis Vuitton announced three new fragrances inspired by the art and life of the late Keith Haring.

“Three fragrances, three ways to let the imagination speak,” reads a somewhat cryptic press release. 

A scent named Attrape-Rêves is described as “a radiant, optimistic fragrance that carries the promise embodied by the ‘radiant baby ,’ Keith Haring’s emblem.” In another scent named Imagination, “the artist’s celebrated characters come alive through the glass of the bottle and its case. They carry the idea that everyone holds an infinite field of possibilities within, and they also appear on the matching travel case in coated Monogram canvas.” 

The final fragrance, Ombre Nomade, is characterized as “a golden labyrinth, with no beginning or end, its lines echoing the swirls of oud wood.” (There’s nary a mention of the smells of a graffiti-strewn 1980s–era subway station, as one might expect.)

The fragrances will be up for sale at Louis Vuitton stores starting January 1, when the rest of the fashion house’s Keith Haring line is made available. The line was inspired in part by a garment case on which Haring painted his radiant baby decades before Nicolas Ghesquière, Louis Vuitton’s artistic director of women’s collections, included it in his Cruise 2027 Show staged at the Frick Collection in New York, as part of a three-year partnership between the brand and the museum.
items.t: Louis Vuitton Launches Three Fragrances as Part of Expansive Keith Haring Collection

items.title: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
items.summary:
Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.

Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative. 

Installation view of Olivia Reavey: Distention at Thomas Erben Gallery (photo courtesy Thomas Erben Gallery)
items.t: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality

items.title: Amid Legal Controversy, Christie’s Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction
items.summary:
Christie’s pulled a Frida Kahlo painting from an evening sale hours before it was to be auctioned amid a debate over whether the work was legally permitted to leave Mexico.

“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research. We look forward to selling this work at a later date,” a spokesperson for Christie’s told ARTnews . The work, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $2 million to $3.5 million, was to be included in the 20th Century Evening Sale in New York, scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. on November 17.

In the days leading up to the sale, Mexico’s cultural authorities had faced accusations of failing to protect the painting, which is considered part of nation’s heritage and legally protected. An online campaign argued that the 1952 work, titled Congreso de los pueblos por la paz ( Congress of the Peoples for Peace ), was part of the trust that Kahlo’s husband, the artist Diego Rivera, created for the Casa Azul after her death in 1954 and that it cannot legally leave the country. It is unclear where the painting was held prior to it coming to New York for this week’s auction.

The Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews that the painting is part of an ongoing investigation by Mexican authorities. At the time of publication, the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL), which is responsible for the country’s patrimony, maintained that Kahlo donated it during her lifetime and that it left Mexico before her work was declared an artistic monument in 1984.

In a statement Monday, the collective behind the campaign,…
items.t: Amid Legal Controversy, Christie’s Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction

items.title: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
items.summary:
Natalie White, “You Should’ve Seen it in Color” (2024), Giant Polaroid (image courtesy the artist) WHATELY, Mass. — The text message said to head around back to the barn, an only slightly ominous-looking structure with heavily weathered wooden siding, tucked off a winding road in Franklin County, Massachusetts. Inside was one of the world’s only 20x24 Polaroid Land Cameras — sometimes referred to as the Giant Polaroid — and the artist Natalie White, shooting with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film long past its expiration date.

A muse and model-turned-photographer, performance artist, and feminist activist, White just debuted 15 of her unique large-format Polaroids in Natalie White: Strange Magick , a selling exhibition at Phillips Los Angeles. The images are colorful and dreamy, close-up portraits of the artist with an otherworldly quality. Each photo is a double exposure, an unpredictable process that creates ghostly effects with White’s hands and fingers overlaid atop her face.

To achieve this, White leaves the film in the camera after pushing the shutter, takes a second shot, and hopes for the best. 

“We’re giving all control to the negative,” White told Hyperallergic . “We always joke that there’s a little magical man painting inside the camera who decides what the double exposure is going to look like.”
items.t: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer

items.title: The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement
items.summary:
Fluorescent foliage, crisp breezes, dogs in sweaters, and international museum partnership announcements — one of these is not like the others, but you can check them all off on this autumn's bingo card. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan and the Shanghai Museum have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) codifying their relationship ahead of a dual-collection historic jewelry exhibition opening at the Shanghai institution this week. 

The MoU between the two museums was announced less than three weeks after the Museum of Modern Art, Centre Pompidou in Paris, and M+ Museum in Hong Kong publicized their collections alliance at the end of October, further illustrating an institutional shift toward resource pooling, joint acquisitions, and other collaboration initiatives popularized in the wake of pandemic-induced budget deficits. 

The Met and the Shanghai Museum, which have worked together on myriad projects and exhibitions since 1980, stated in a press release that their shared goals in scholarship and presentation advancement will manifest through “exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange.”
items.t: The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement

items.title: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts
items.summary:
Last month, just a couple of weeks before Ouattara Watts’s solo show opened at Karma, I was directed to knock on the cracked glass door of his Bushwick studio. We met in the late afternoon, which is when his studio time begins. The Ivorian-American artist has coffee and a light evening meal, and works all night, before returning home to sleep during the day. To learn why Watts works only at night, one need only look at his paintings. He views art as a portal to the divine; night is when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest, and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest. 

Although a gallery representative had told me Watts would be putting “finishing touches” on the paintings for his exhibition at the time of our meeting, I came to realize that he thinks about the work, and his process, without a beginning or end. The centrifugal energy of his rhythmic compositions does not obey edges. Totemic forms continue beyond the bounds of the canvases; arrows point in varying directions; seed pods are split open to reveal concentric circles. His compositions are stained and dripped fields populated by a lexicon of imagery and symbols, developed over the past four decades. They include coffee beans, sacred books, musical notes, serpents, bursting petals encased in atoms, diagrammatic cubes, and mathematical codes. 

Ouattara Watts, “Love Supreme” (2026), mixed media on canvas (© Ouattara Watts; image courtesy the artist and Karma)
items.t: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts

items.title: Cologne Auction House Moves Forward with Sale of Gothic Paintings as Jewish Dealer’s Heirs Claim They Were ‘Stolen’
items.summary:
The Cologne-based Lempertz auction house said it still planned to sell two works by Gothic painter Johann Koerbecke after the heirs of a German Jewish art dealer who was persecuted by the Nazis claimed the pieces were “stolen.”

Dealer Max Stern held the paintings in Düsseldorf between 1936 and 1937, the year the Nazis shut down his gallery. Per a provenance supplied by Lempertz, both paintings were then held by Düsseldorf’s Galerie Hans Bammann, which appears to have then sold them.

On Monday, the Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation issued a release in which it called on Lempertz to stop the sale of the two works planned for Saturday. According to the foundation, such a sale should not occur “until two distinct ownership claims of different victims are justly resolved according to the Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.”

Both paintings— The Annunciation and The Vision of Saint Bernard —are likely from Marienfeld high altarpiece, which was completed in 1457. They are being auctioned in a sale of Old Masters art. They carry high estimates of around 300,000 euros each, or about $329,000 apiece, making them the auction’s most expensive works. “For art historical reasons,” the Lempertz lot entries read, “the two important panels (Lots 1005 and 1006) will first be offered individually and then together.”

The Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation pointed out that both works appear in several databases of missing artworks, including the Interpol Database of Stolen Art since 2021. On the German Lost Art Database, both are reported as “Nazi-confiscated property”; the…
items.t: Cologne Auction House Moves Forward with Sale of Gothic Paintings as Jewish Dealer’s Heirs Claim They Were ‘Stolen’

items.title: Celebrating the Inaugural Art Week NYC, Organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum
items.summary:
ARTnews , Art in America , and Artforum just wrapped up the inaugural edition of Art Week NYC , a citywide event celebrating all the New York art world’s ecosystem has to offer, from museums and galleries to artists, collectors, and cultural tastemakers from the Lower East Side and Tribeca to Chelsea and the Upper East Side.

Art Week NYC kicked off with an opening party at the Mallory in Chelsea, a 19th-century warehouse building that used to be home to the Tunnel nightclub. Programming took place over four jampacked days, from November 11–14. A launch event at the Metropolitan Museum of Art had in attendance New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, City Council Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal; New York State Senator Jose Serrano, and City Council member Virginia Maloney. David Breslin, the Met’s curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, referred to Art Week NYC as “a defining tradition in our city’s cultural landscape—and that’s saying a lot.”

On November 13 and 14, ARTnews hosted a slate of programming at PMC’s ground-floor studio across the street from the New York Public Library. The two-day event was presented by Amazon, in partnership with Louis Roederer Champagne, Piaget, and Flying Whale Wines. 

Friday featured in-depth conversations with art world insiders, such as dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky on what separates collectors from speculators; Tina Vaz, the MTA’s director of arts and design, speaking about several newly announced public art commissions; and photographer Stephen…

items.title: New Museum Inks Multiyear Partnership with Video Art–Focused Vega Foundation
items.summary:
As part of its expanded programming at its recently enlarged New York home, the New Museum is launching a multiyear partnership with the Vega Foundation, an organization known for supporting major video art commissions that was launched by Elisa Nuyten, a board member.

The foundation has a reputation for providing opportunities to emerging and mid-career artists working in film and video , two mediums that are under-supported and difficult to monetize. Artists to have received Vega commissions include Ali Cherri, Diego Marcon, Martine Syms, and Yuyan Wang. (Marcon is currently the subject of a New Museum show that features a reformulated Vega Foundation commission.) Based in Toronto and begun in 2022, the Vega Foundation has often brought its commissions to Canada’s institutions; that will happen once again with the New Museum’s commissions.

“The New Museum has played such an important role in making space for new forms of art and ideas, and I hope this partnership will build on that history,” Nuyten, a recent addition to ARTnews ’s Top 200 Collectors list , said in an email. “Just as importantly, I hope these projects will have lives beyond their initial presentations in New York. Bringing this work to Canadian audiences is central to what we do at Vega.”

She continued, “For Vega, supporting artists also means thinking about how their work continues to reach new audiences and find new contexts over time. That’s something I’d really like to see come out of this partnership.”

items.title: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act
items.summary:
The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.

Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “ the death mask of America .”

NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.
items.t: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act

items.title: Who Gets Remembered in Art History? New Free Online Course Explores Women Who Shaped Indonesian Art
items.summary:
How have women artists shaped Indonesia's cultural, social, and artistic histories? National Gallery Singapore's new free online course, Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower , co-developed with independent curator Alia Swastika, explores this question through the practices and perspectives of leading contemporary artists.   

Screenshot image from Art as Resistance by National Gallery Singapore (2026) “The absence of women [in historical accounts] does not necessarily indicate a lack of participation.” — Alia Swastika

The course underscores the importance of recovering women’s contributions and bringing overlooked figures and landmark events into view. 

Through the work of artists from different generations, regions, and artistic backgrounds, Art and Women in Indonesia highlights a plurality of experiences and perspectives, offering new ways of understanding Indonesia’s histories and their continued resonance in the present. 

Structured over five weeks, the course explores the practices of six artists and one collective whose work spans painting, sculpture, installation, performances, and collaborative forms. Together, they illuminate the diverse ways women have contributed to Indonesia’s cultural landscape while engaging questions of memory, power, gender, spirituality, and resistance. 

Featured artists include Arahmaiani and Dolorosa Sinaga, whose works confront authoritarianism, censorship, conservatism, and the politics of the female body in public space. Through distinct artistic approaches, they expose the mechanisms through which women’s lives are…

items.title: Anawana Haloba Chosen for Tate Modern’s 2027 Infinities Commission
items.summary:
Anawana Haloba will become the third artist to create a major new work as part of Tate Modern’s Infinities Commission. to be unveiled in June 2027, the commission will be installed in the Tanks, massive underground spaces that once held the oil that fueled the former power station and are now dedicated to experimental forms of performance, installation, and time-based media.

Haloba, who was born in Zambia in 1978, creates video, performance, and sculptural installations using sound, music, oral tradition, and storytelling, including African opera, ritual, and philosophy. In this way, she explores how history is remembered and reimagined, while often reflecting on the continued impact of colonialism on society. She is based between Zambia and Norway, and has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art in Washington, D.C., as well as the Venice Biennale.

“Anawana Haloba is an exceptional artist whose boundary-pushing, interdisciplinary work brings together sound, storytelling, performance and installation in profoundly affecting ways,” Catherine Wood, Tate Modern’s interim director, said in a press release. “We are delighted to support her in creating a visionary new work for the Tanks.”

Past winners of the commission since its launch in 2025 have included Christelle Oyiri and nora chipaumire .

Additionally, Tate’s panel of judges—chaired by Charmaine Toh, acting head of curatorial at Tate Modern-has selected three emerging artists to receive a £10,000 ($13,195) grant for research and development. They are Saudi Arabian artist…
items.t: Anawana Haloba Chosen for Tate Modern’s 2027 Infinities Commission

items.title: ‘Dolls deserve complex roles’: the trans theatre troupe turning Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
items.summary:
A radical new take on Virginia Woolf’s modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations

As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?”

Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals, a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.”

Continue reading...

items.title: Sotheby’s, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale
items.summary:
Sotheby’s has reached an agreement with the heirs of a Jewish publisher who challenged the sale of a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting last week, clearing the way for the picture to go under the hammer Wednesday night.

The auction house said Tuesday that the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) since 1975, reached a settlement with all the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer. The terms weren’t disclosed, but Sotheby’s confirmed to ARTnews that the agreement resolves the ownership claims and that the painting’s buyer will receive clear title.

The deal brings an end to a messy public brawl that erupted last Thursday in the pages of the New York Times , just six days before the painting was due to lead Sotheby’s $450 million sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection.

As the Times first reported , the Fischer heirs argued that their family had been forced to sell the painting in Amsterdam in 1936 because of financial pressures brought on by Nazi persecution. Their Berlin lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, demanded Sotheby’s withdraw the work from sale unless it could establish that the transaction had been voluntary.

Sotheby’s disputed that account. As ARTnews reported on Sunday the auction house said records from the archives of the art dealer Paul Cassirer showed that the painting sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, or approximately $22,000, in June 1936. Sotheby’s maintained that this was a fair price for a van Gogh at the time, and that the picture had been in Amsterdam for nearly three years before its sale.

The timing of…
items.t: Sotheby’s, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale

items.title: For Abi Palmer, Chronic Illness Is Like Being an Indoor Cat
items.summary:
“I have been trying so hard to capture the smell of rain for you,” an unseen narrator with a British accent explains in Abi Palmer Invents the Weather (2023), as cats slink across the screen. “But being as I am no god or scientist,” the voice continues, as human hands wring out a cloth soaking in a jar of dirty water, “I am forced to work backward.” Soon, dripping white fabric is seen hanging from twine inside a cardboard box, clumped like a cloud.

Abi Palmer: Abi Palmer Invents the Weather , 2023. 

Courtesy Abi Palmer 

This non-god, the artist Abi Palmer, is recreating the weather for her two indoor cats, mixing rainwater with moss and earth. All the while, she muses on how chronic illness keeps her inside, catlike, yet also binds her intricately to meteorological variation. Palmer alludes to the ways joint pain can flare when pressure drops or smoky skies are felt by some in the lungs or in the back of the throat.

As it happens, Palmer got her start making art in the form of wet white wads. As an “unsupervised child,” as she told me from her London apartment, she’d combine water and tissue into globby sculptures—“blob creatures”—then let them dry. Recently, making massive slug sculptures inspired by the way the species survives by ugliness, she realized how consistent her materials and methods remained. At the University of Cambridge, she studied literature, as is evident in her voice-overs and her two books: Sanitorium (2020) and Slugs: A Manifesto (2024). But soon, she found her hands hurt too much to type—though her muscles were “really bendy” and thus “good at…
items.t: For Abi Palmer, Chronic Illness Is Like Being an Indoor Cat

items.title: Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, and Dawoud Bey Enter MCA Chicago Collection Through 65-Work Gift
items.summary:
The Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago has received a promised gift of 65 artworks from longtime supporters Jack and Sandra Guthman to mark its 60th anniversary.

The gift from the Chicago-based collectors spans paintings, photography, works on paper, and sculptures, and includes works by Pope.L, Gary Simmons, Andrea Bowers, Christian Marclay, Elle Pérez, and Shinique Smith. The museum said in a release that the selected works were chosen in tandem with the curatorial staff, “taking the MCA’s collecting priorities into serious consideration.”

In its announcement, the MCA Chicago reported that, of the 54 artists represented in the gift, 23 (or 43 percent) are people of color, 19 (or 35 percente) are women, and 13 are entering the collection for the first time, among them Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, Dawoud Bey, and Amanda Williams. Johnson’s traveling survey, which opened at the Guggenheim Museum last year, is currently on view at the MCA Chicago; Williams will have a solo show at the museum next year.

“Together, Jack and Sandy have helped shape Chicago’s cultural life through their collecting, advocacy, and longstanding engagement with artists and institutions,” MCA Chicago director Madeleine Grynsztejn said in a statement. “To be entrusted with this tremendous gift is a great honor.”

The Guthmans first donated an artwork to the museum in 1988, and Jack joined the board of trustees the year after. To mark its 50th anniversary in 2016, they donated work by 50 women-identifying photographers, which was the subject of the exhibition “Woman With a Camera.” With the…

items.title: Latinx Art’s New Visionaries
items.summary:
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

items.title: The play that changed my life: ‘John Berger’s Pig Earth became something magical – they licked milk off bodies’
items.summary:
The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol by Complicité conjured the struggles of a French village with an intense rawness

There are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies.

The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company.

items.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
items.summary:
Willem de Kooning, “Yellow River” (1958) (image courtesy Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026) Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million. 

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy . In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections. 

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic 's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

items.title: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
items.summary:
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015,…
items.t: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi

items.title: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
items.summary:
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful. 

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them. 

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows. 

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous…
items.t: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

items.title: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
items.summary:
Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.

Over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.

Sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like…
items.t: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

items.title: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?
items.summary:
These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?

Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away , a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip. 

Film still of Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff “Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.
items.t: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?

items.title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
items.summary:
Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force?

I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet. 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton. 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express.

Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production.

items.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
items.summary:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

items.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
items.summary:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions.

items.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
items.summary:
The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results

According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music.

You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets, which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface.
